Some qualities, like politeness or helpfulness, are hard to capture with labeled "correct answers". **RLHF** teaches them from human preferences instead.
The steps:
- The model generates two or more responses to the same prompt.
- Human reviewers **rank** or pick the better response, for example the polite one over the rude one.
- A separate **reward model** is trained on those rankings so it can predict which response a human would prefer.
- The FM is then trained with reinforcement learning to produce responses that score highly with the reward model.
Example: two correct answers, "Read the manual." and "Happy to help. You can reset it under Settings > Security." Reviewers prefer the second; after RLHF the model answers in that style by default.
RLHF is a main reason chat models are more helpful and harmless than raw pretrained models.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data augmentation:** creates extra training examples by transforming existing ones, such as paraphrasing; it does not use human rankings or a reward model.
- ✗ **B. Few-shot prompting:** puts a few examples in the prompt at inference time; it trains nothing and uses no reward model.
- ✗ **C. Continued pretraining:** trains on unlabeled text with the next-token objective to add domain knowledge; it has no human preference rankings.
- ✓ **D. RLHF (correct):** human reviewers ranking pairs of responses, a reward model learned from those rankings and further training guided by it is exactly the RLHF process, and it is well suited to fixing tone.

## Key idea
Human preference rankings plus a reward model means RLHF; it shapes tone and helpfulness rather than adding knowledge.
Q000090:
## Knowledge in the weights versus knowledge in the prompt
Fine-tuning stores knowledge in the model's weights. Anything that changes after training, like today's stock count, is outdated until you train again, and each fine-tuning run costs time and money.
**Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)** keeps the model unchanged and fetches current data at request time:
- The user asks "Is the blue jacket in stock in size M?"
- The app queries the inventory source (a database, API or a vector index of documents).
- The retrieved facts are added to the prompt, and the FM answers from them.
When inventory changes, only the data source is updated; the next question already sees the new values. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides managed RAG over documents and can also query structured data sources, and Bedrock Agents can call APIs for live values.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fine-tuning:** bakes information into the weights, so daily-changing inventory would need a new training job every day, which is exactly what the company cannot afford.
- ✓ **B. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) (correct):** it supplies the latest data at query time without retraining, so daily changes are reflected immediately at a fraction of the cost of repeated fine-tuning.
- ✗ **C. Model distillation:** produces a smaller copy of a larger model to cut inference cost; the student still only knows what it was trained on and goes stale the same way.
- ✗ **D. Full pretraining:** builds a model from scratch with massive data and compute, the most expensive option, and its knowledge is frozen at training time as well.

## Key idea
Frequently changing facts belong in retrieval (RAG), not in the weights; any training-based method goes stale as soon as the data changes.
Q000091:
## What automatic metrics miss
Automatic metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE or BERTScore compare model output to reference text. They are fast and cheap, but they cannot tell whether an answer:
- Sounds friendly or condescending
- Actually helps the customer resolve the problem
- Matches the company's brand voice and policies
Two chatbot versions can score the same while customers clearly prefer one.
## Human evaluation
Reviewers (internal experts or crowd workers) read responses and rate them on criteria such as helpfulness, tone, correctness and brand fit, or pick the better of two responses side by side. The results show which version people actually prefer.
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation supports human evaluation jobs in which your own work team rates or compares responses, alongside automatic evaluation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Checking GPU utilization during generation:** measures infrastructure load; it says nothing about how customers perceive the content of answers.
- ✓ **B. Human evaluation by reviewers (correct):** people can judge subjective qualities like tone, helpfulness and brand fit that the automatic scores missed, explaining why customers prefer one version.
- ✗ **C. Measuring token counts only:** shows response length and cost, not whether the response is helpful or on-brand.
- ✗ **D. Comparing model file sizes:** reflects model size and deployment footprint; two versions of any size can differ in tone and helpfulness.

## Key idea
When metrics tie but people disagree, use human evaluation for subjective qualities; infrastructure and size numbers do not measure answer quality.
Q000092:
## What a benchmark dataset is
A **benchmark** is a fixed, public set of tasks with known answers and a defined scoring method, for example question answering, summarization or reasoning sets. Because every model is run on the same inputs and scored the same way, results are comparable and repeatable.
## Benchmarks plus your own tests
- **Benchmarks** give a fair, standardized baseline: model X scores 82 and model Y scores 76 on the same test, and anyone rerunning it gets the same comparison.
- **Your own tests** use your real prompts and data, which is what finally matters for your use case.
A benchmark winner is not guaranteed to win on your task, because benchmarks may not match your domain and models may have seen public benchmark data during training. That is why teams use both. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation offers built-in datasets and also accepts your own prompt dataset.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Consistent, repeatable comparison on the same tasks (correct):** a standardized benchmark evaluates all three models on identical inputs with the same scoring, giving an objective baseline alongside the team's own tests.
- ✗ **B. It guarantees the best benchmark model wins in production:** benchmarks do not reflect your specific data and users, so a top benchmark score is no guarantee of the best production result.
- ✗ **C. It trains the models to be more accurate:** evaluation only measures models; running a benchmark does not change any weights.
- ✗ **D. It removes the need for any business testing:** generic benchmarks cannot confirm fit for your prompts, data and requirements, so business-specific testing is still required.

## Key idea
Benchmarks give comparable, repeatable scores; they measure but do not train, and they complement rather than replace testing on your own use case.
Q000093:
## Amazon Bedrock model evaluation
Picking the right FM means comparing candidates on your own prompts. Amazon Bedrock includes a managed evaluation feature so you do not have to build scripts, scoring logic and reviewer tools yourself.
Evaluation options:
- **Automatic (programmatic)**: runs the prompts through each model and computes metrics such as accuracy, robustness and toxicity, using built-in datasets or your own prompt dataset in Amazon S3.
- **Model as a judge**: another FM scores responses on criteria like correctness, completeness and helpfulness.
- **Human evaluation**: human reviewers from your own work team rate or compare responses.
Results are stored as reports, so you can compare models side by side, for example three models on 500 support questions, and pick the best one for cost and quality.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Model Evaluation in Amazon Bedrock (correct):** it is the built-in feature for comparing FMs on the same prompts with automatic metrics or human evaluators, without custom tooling.
- ✗ **B. Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock:** provides managed RAG by connecting models to your documents; it does not run evaluation jobs comparing models.
- ✗ **C. Agents for Amazon Bedrock:** orchestrates multi-step tasks and tool calls for an application; it is for building workflows, not scoring model outputs.
- ✗ **D. Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock:** filters and restricts inputs and outputs for safety; it enforces policies but does not compare model quality.

## Key idea
Comparing FMs with metrics or human reviewers is Bedrock model evaluation; Knowledge Bases, Agents and Guardrails are building blocks of the application itself.
Q000094:
## ROUGE for summaries
**ROUGE** (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) compares a generated summary with one or more human-written reference summaries by counting overlapping **n-grams** (sequences of n words).
- **ROUGE-1** counts overlapping single words, **ROUGE-2** overlapping word pairs.
- **ROUGE-L** uses the longest common subsequence, rewarding matching word order.
- It is recall oriented: it asks how much of the reference content appears in the generated summary, which suits summarization, where covering the key points matters.
Example: reference "the company reported record profits", generated "the company reported strong profits". Four of the five reference words also appear in the generated summary, so ROUGE-1 recall is 4/5 = 0.8.
Limitation: ROUGE rewards identical wording; a good paraphrase using different words scores low.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Classification F1 score:** combines precision and recall of predicted class labels; it evaluates classification, not the overlap of words in generated text.
- ✗ **B. BERTScore:** compares texts by embedding similarity, capturing meaning even with different words, rather than counting exact n-gram overlap.
- ✓ **C. ROUGE (correct):** it is the standard summarization metric that measures n-gram overlap between the generated summary and human reference summaries.
- ✗ **D. BLEU:** also counts n-gram overlap, but it is precision oriented and was designed for machine translation; the metric commonly associated with summaries is ROUGE.

## Key idea
n-gram overlap with reference summaries means ROUGE (recall, summarization); BLEU is the precision-based translation counterpart and BERTScore compares meaning.
Q000095:
## BLEU for translation
**BLEU** (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) scores machine translation by comparing the generated translation with one or more human reference translations.
How it works:
- It counts how many of the generated **n-grams** (1 to usually 4 words) also appear in the references. That is **precision**: of what the model wrote, how much matches a reference.
- It combines these precisions and applies a **brevity penalty** so very short outputs cannot score well by writing only a few safe words.
- Scores range from 0 to 1 (often shown as 0 to 100); higher means closer to the references.
Example: reference "the cat sits on the mat", output "the cat is on the mat". Most words and several word pairs match, so BLEU is fairly high, but "is" versus "sits" lowers it.
Like ROUGE, BLEU only sees surface wording, so valid alternative translations can be under-scored.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. BERTScore:** measures semantic similarity with contextual embeddings rather than counting n-gram matches.
- ✗ **B. ROUGE:** also counts n-gram overlap, but it is recall oriented and mainly used for summarization, not a precision-based translation metric.
- ✗ **C. Perplexity:** measures how well a language model predicts text (how "surprised" it is); it does not compare output to reference translations at all.
- ✓ **D. BLEU (correct):** a precision-based n-gram overlap metric designed for comparing machine translations with human references, exactly as described.

## Key idea
Precision-based n-gram overlap for translation is BLEU; ROUGE is the recall-oriented summarization counterpart and perplexity needs no reference.
Q000096:
## Measuring meaning instead of exact words
Metrics like BLEU and ROUGE count identical words. They punish a correct answer that simply uses different wording.
**BERTScore** fixes this with a pretrained language model such as BERT:
- Each word (token) in the generated text and in the reference is turned into a **contextual embedding**, a vector that represents the word's meaning in that sentence.
- Words are matched to their most similar words in the other text using cosine similarity.
- Those similarities are combined into precision, recall and F1 scores.
Example: reference "The film was excellent", generated "The movie was outstanding". Few exact words match, so BLEU is low, but "film"/"movie" and "excellent"/"outstanding" have close embeddings, so BERTScore stays high.
Amazon Bedrock automatic model evaluation uses BERTScore for some built-in metrics, for example accuracy on text summarization tasks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. BLEU:** counts exact n-gram matches with a precision focus, so different words with the same meaning are not credited.
- ✗ **B. ROUGE:** counts exact n-gram overlap with a recall focus; it has no notion of semantic similarity between different words.
- ✓ **C. BERTScore (correct):** it uses contextual embeddings from a pretrained language model to compare generated and reference text semantically, so paraphrases still score well.
- ✗ **D. Exact match accuracy:** gives credit only when the output is identical to the reference, the strictest surface-level comparison possible.

## Key idea
Embedding-based semantic similarity is BERTScore; BLEU, ROUGE and exact match all depend on identical words.
Q000097:
## Using a model to grade a model
Human reviewers judge quality well but cannot read thousands of long answers quickly or cheaply. Word-overlap metrics are cheap but cannot judge coherence or helpfulness.
**LLM-as-a-judge** sits in between: a strong FM is given a grading prompt with clear criteria and scores each response.
Example judge prompt: "Rate the answer below from 1 to 5 for coherence and for helpfulness to the user's question. Explain the score." The judge returns scores and reasons for each of the thousands of responses in minutes.
- Captures nuanced qualities such as logic, relevance and completeness.
- Scales to large volumes at low cost.
- Best practice: check a sample against human ratings to confirm the judge agrees with people.
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation offers model-as-a-judge evaluation jobs with built-in and custom metrics.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data poisoning detection:** is about finding malicious data in training sets; it does not score response quality.
- ✓ **B. LLM-as-a-judge (correct):** an FM scores responses against criteria like coherence and helpfulness, giving nuanced judgments at a scale and cost human review cannot match.
- ✗ **C. BLEU scoring only:** measures word overlap with reference texts, which is exactly the "simple word overlap" the company wants to go beyond, and long-form answers often have no single reference.
- ✗ **D. Exact string matching:** only checks whether output is identical to an expected string, useless for judging free-form long answers.

## Key idea
For nuanced quality at scale without human reviewers, use an LLM as the judge; overlap and exact-match metrics only compare wording.
Q000098:
## Two parts of a RAG system to evaluate
A RAG application has a **retriever** that finds documents and a **generator** (the FM) that writes the answer from them. An answer can fail because of either part, so both need evaluation.
- **Retrieval relevance**: did the search return the right passages for the question? If the user asks about the refund policy and the retriever returns the shipping policy, even a perfect model gives a poor answer.
- **Groundedness (faithfulness)**: is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved passages, or did the model add unsupported information (hallucinate)?
- Standard FM checks such as correctness and helpfulness still apply to the final answer.
A standalone FM has no retrieval step, so these checks exist only for RAG. Amazon Bedrock evaluations can evaluate Knowledge Bases on retrieval quality (for example context relevance and coverage) and on retrieve-and-generate quality (for example faithfulness).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Counting the number of fine-tuning epochs used:** is a training setting, and a RAG system typically does not fine-tune at all; it says nothing about retrieval quality.
- ✗ **B. Measuring inference latency exclusively:** latency matters for any FM application, so it is not unique to RAG, and measuring it alone ignores whether retrieved documents are relevant.
- ✗ **C. Measuring only the model's temperature setting:** temperature is a configuration value, not an evaluation result, and it does not reveal whether retrieval worked.
- ✓ **D. Retrieval relevance and answer groundedness (correct):** these measure whether retrieved documents fit the query and whether the answer stays true to them, which only applies to systems with a retrieval step.

## Key idea
RAG adds a retrieval step, so its unique evaluations are whether the right context was retrieved and whether the answer is grounded in it.
Q000099:
## Evaluating an agent, not just a response
An AI agent works in a loop: it plans steps, calls tools or APIs, reads the results and decides what to do next until the request is done.
Example: "Change my flight to Friday and email me the receipt" needs finding the booking, checking availability, rebooking, and sending an email.
A single good-looking reply does not mean the job was done. Agent evaluation focuses on:
- **Task completion**: was the whole goal achieved end to end?
- **Tool use**: did the agent pick the correct tools and pass correct parameters?
- **Trajectory**: were the steps sensible and efficient, without loops or unnecessary calls?
- Safety and error handling when a tool fails.
Task completion is the headline metric, because an agent that writes polite messages but never rebooks the flight has failed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. The ROUGE score of only the agent's first response:** measures word overlap of one message and ignores every later step, tool call and the final outcome.
- ✗ **B. The storage capacity of the vector database used:** is an infrastructure sizing detail; it tells you nothing about whether the agent performed the task correctly.
- ✓ **C. Whether the agent completes the whole multi-step task (correct):** agentic systems are judged on reaching the end goal across planning and tool calls, which single-response evaluation cannot capture.
- ✗ **D.:** The temperature parameter used during the model's original pretraining: temperature is an inference setting, not a pretraining result, and it does not measure agent behavior.

## Key idea
Agents are evaluated on end-to-end task completion and correct tool use, not on the wording of a single response.
Q000100:
## Model metrics versus business metrics
BLEU and ROUGE are **model quality metrics**: they measure how closely generated text matches reference text. Improvements there do not prove the chatbot creates business value.
**Business metrics** connect the AI to outcomes leadership cares about:
- **Task completion rate**: share of conversations where the customer's issue was resolved without a human, for example 62% resolved end to end.
- **Cost per interaction**: total cost of model calls and infrastructure divided by conversations, compared with the cost of a human agent handling the same contact.
- Others: customer satisfaction (CSAT), escalation rate, average handle time and conversion rate.
Example: if task completion rises from 55% to 70% and each interaction costs well below a human-handled contact, leadership can see the return on investment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Task completion rate and cost per interaction (correct):** they measure whether customers actually get their problems solved and at what cost, which directly shows business value.
- ✗ **B. Model parameter count and context window size:** describe the model's technical specifications, not whether it helps customers or saves money.
- ✗ **C. BLEU score on a new dataset:** is still a text-similarity metric of the same kind leadership is questioning, so it adds no evidence of business impact.
- ✗ **D. Perplexity and token entropy:** measure how confidently the model predicts text; they are technical indicators with no direct link to revenue, cost or customer outcomes.

## Key idea
To show business value, measure outcomes like task completion and cost per interaction; text-similarity and model specs only describe technical quality.
Q000101:
## What BLEU and ROUGE actually measure
BLEU and ROUGE are automatic metrics that count overlapping n-grams (short word sequences) between a model's output and a reference answer.
- **BLEU** is precision-oriented: how many of the generated n-grams appear in the reference. It came from machine translation.
- **ROUGE** is recall-oriented: how much of the reference is covered by the output. It came from summarization.
## Why overlap is not the same as usefulness
Suppose the reference answer is "Reset your password from the account settings page." A reply of "You can reset your password from the settings page of your account, but first contact billing" scores high overlap, yet the extra step may be wrong and unhelpful. N-gram metrics do not check factual correctness, whether the customer's real question was answered, tone, or whether the reply is actionable.
- Good practice combines automatic metrics with **human evaluation** (for example rating helpfulness and correctness) and, on AWS, model evaluation jobs in Amazon Bedrock that support human reviewers or an LLM-as-a-judge.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inverse correlation with accuracy:** higher BLEU or ROUGE means more overlap with a reference, which generally points toward, not away from, the reference answer. The problem is that overlap is an incomplete signal, not that it runs backward.
- ✗ **B. Temperature necessarily zero:** nothing in the scenario forces temperature to zero, and a deterministic temperature would not by itself explain unhappy users when test metrics were strong.
- ✗ **C. Unencrypted knowledge base:** encryption at rest protects data from unauthorized access; it has no effect on answer quality or on how customers rate the chatbot's replies.
- ✓ **D. N-gram metrics miss real usefulness (correct):** high word overlap with reference answers can coexist with replies that are incorrect, incomplete or unhelpful to real customers, so human review of helpfulness and correctness is needed alongside BLEU and ROUGE.

## Key idea
BLEU and ROUGE measure word overlap with references, not helpfulness or correctness, so pair them with human evaluation before trusting them.
Q000102:
## The responsible AI dimensions AWS describes
AWS groups responsible AI into several dimensions, including fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, **veracity and robustness**, governance and transparency.
## Veracity: getting the facts right
Veracity means the system produces correct, truthful output. For generative AI the main threat is **hallucination**: fluent text that is confidently wrong.
- A medical FAQ bot that says a medication dose is "twice daily" when the approved leaflet says "once daily" fails veracity even if the wording is polite and unbiased.
- Typical controls are grounding answers in approved content with retrieval-augmented generation (for example Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases), contextual grounding checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and evaluating answers against a verified test set.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Controllability:** controllability is about being able to monitor and steer the system's behavior (for example keeping it on task); it does not by itself guarantee the facts it states are correct.
- ✗ **B. Privacy:** privacy concerns how personal data is collected, used and protected, not whether the bot's medical statements are true.
- ✗ **C. Fairness across demographic groups:** fairness asks whether outcomes are equitable across groups; a bot could treat every group equally and still give the same wrong answer to all of them.
- ✓ **D. Veracity (truthfulness and accuracy) (correct):** the requirement is that answers be factually correct and grounded in approved content, which is exactly what the veracity dimension covers.

## Key idea
Correct, grounded answers are a veracity requirement; fairness, privacy and controllability address different risks.
Q000103:
## Robustness: stable behavior on messy inputs
Robustness is part of the AWS "veracity and robustness" dimension. A robust model keeps giving reliable output when inputs change in small, realistic ways: typos, different phrasing, extra whitespace, casing, or slightly noisy data.
## How the weakness shows up
- "How do I reset my password?" gets a correct answer, but "how do i rest my pasword" or "I forgot my login secret, what now?" gets a wrong or nonsensical one.
- The model has learned surface patterns of clean training examples rather than the underlying intent.
## How teams improve it
- Test with perturbed inputs (typos, paraphrases, adversarial prompts) as part of evaluation; SageMaker Clarify and Bedrock model evaluation include robustness-style tests for foundation models.
- Add varied, noisy examples to training or fine-tuning data, and monitor production inputs for drift.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Explainability:** explainability is about understanding why a model produced an output; an explainable model can still break on misspelled inputs.
- ✗ **B. Governance:** governance covers policies, oversight, approvals and accountability for AI systems; it is an organizational process, not a property of how the model reacts to noisy text.
- ✗ **C. Transparency:** transparency means disclosing how the system works, its data and limits; being transparent does not make the model tolerate typos.
- ✓ **D. Robustness (correct):** failing badly on typos and slight rephrasing while succeeding on clean inputs is the textbook sign of a model that is not robust to input variation.

## Key idea
Good results only on clean inputs point to missing robustness; transparency and explainability are about understanding the model, not its stability.
Q000104:
## Two distinct generative AI risks
- **Intellectual property (IP) infringement**: a model trained on, or reproducing, copyrighted material without permission can expose the company to legal claims. The harm is legal and financial, and the cause is how content was sourced or reproduced.
- **Hallucination**: the model generates plausible but false statements, such as describing a product feature that does not exist. Repeated hallucinations lead to **loss of trust**: customers stop believing anything the assistant says.
## Matching cause to effect
Trust loss is an outcome, not a root cause, and bias is a different problem again (systematically unfair outputs for certain groups).
- Risk 1 (a lawsuit over copyrighted text) is caused by IP infringement.
- Risk 2 (customers losing confidence because features are invented) is caused by hallucination that leads to trust loss.
Mitigations differ: IP risk is handled with licensed data, provenance review and output filtering; hallucination with grounding (RAG), guardrails and human review.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hallucination, then biased outputs:** a copyright lawsuit is not caused by hallucination, and inventing product features is fabrication, not bias against a group.
- ✗ **B. Biased outputs, then IP infringement:** bias concerns unfair treatment of groups, not unauthorized use of copyrighted text, and made-up features do not infringe anyone's IP.
- ✗ **C. Trust loss, then IP infringement:** trust loss is the effect of Risk 2, not the cause of a copyright suit, and invented features are hallucinations rather than IP violations.
- ✓ **D. IP infringement, then hallucination leading to trust loss (correct):** using copyrighted text without authorization is an IP problem, and inventing nonexistent features is hallucination whose consequence is lost customer confidence.

## Key idea
Copyright misuse is an IP risk; invented facts are hallucinations whose consequence is lost trust.
Q000105:
## Where model bias comes from
A model learns patterns from its training data. If the data over-represents some groups or encodes past unfair decisions, the model reproduces them.
- Example: if historical hires were mostly from one university and one gender, a resume screener trained on them learns to prefer those traits.
## Characteristics of a fair training dataset
- **Diverse and representative**: covers the range of candidates the model will actually see, across demographics, backgrounds and career paths.
- **Vetted sources**: data provenance is known and checked for quality, labeling errors and historical bias.
- **Measured, not assumed**: tools such as Amazon SageMaker Clarify can compute pre-training bias metrics (for example class imbalance between groups) before a model is trained.
Removing a sensitive column is not enough, because other fields (zip code, school, hobbies) can act as proxies for it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only highest-performing employees:** this narrows the data to whoever the company already hired and promoted, so any historical bias in those decisions is baked into the model.
- ✗ **B. Drop demographic fields with no review:** other attributes such as location, school or gaps in employment can still act as proxies, and without review the bias is simply hidden rather than removed.
- ✗ **C. Largest dataset regardless of source:** volume does not fix skew; a huge unvetted dataset can be even more unrepresentative or carry more historical bias than a smaller curated one.
- ✓ **D. Diverse, representative examples from vetted sources (correct):** data that reflects the full applicant population and comes from checked sources reduces the chance the model learns patterns that disadvantage any group.

## Key idea
Fairness starts with representative, vetted data; dropping sensitive columns or adding volume alone does not remove bias.
Q000106:
## Why aggregate accuracy can hide problems
Overall accuracy averages across every test example. If one subgroup is small, its errors barely move the average.
- Example: 10,000 test applicants, 9,500 in the majority group at 97% accuracy and 500 in a minority group at 60% accuracy. Overall accuracy is still about 95%.
## Subgroup (disaggregated) analysis
Subgroup analysis computes the same metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, false positive and false negative rates) separately for each segment, such as age band or demographic group, and compares them.
- Large gaps signal that the model does not work equally well for everyone, often because that group was under-represented in training.
- Amazon SageMaker Clarify supports this with post-training bias metrics that compare outcomes and error rates across facets (the groups you choose to compare).
Finding the gap before deployment lets the team collect more data, rebalance or reconsider the model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only overall accuracy:** this is exactly the measurement that hid the problem, because a small subgroup's errors hardly affect the aggregate.
- ✗ **B. Higher learning rate:** the learning rate controls optimization step size during training; changing it does not measure or reveal performance differences between groups.
- ✓ **C. Subgroup analysis of metrics per demographic segment (correct):** computing accuracy for each segment would have revealed the 60% result that the 95% overall number concealed.
- ✗ **D. Fewer training epochs:** reducing epochs changes how long the model trains and may cause underfitting, but it is not a diagnostic that shows per-group accuracy.

## Key idea
Aggregate metrics hide subgroup failures; evaluate metrics per segment before deploying.
Q000107:
## Overfitting in one picture
A model **overfits** when it learns the training data too closely, including noise and quirks, instead of general patterns.
- Symptom: very high training accuracy (98%) but much lower accuracy on new data (70%).
- The opposite, **underfitting**, means the model is too simple: accuracy is poor on training and new data alike.
## Why small groups suffer most
When a group has only a few training examples, the model can effectively memorize those specific records rather than learn what generalizes for that group. On new members of the group, predictions are worst.
- This turns a generalization problem into a fairness problem: the under-represented group gets the least reliable decisions.
- Remedies include more and more representative data, regularization, early stopping, cross-validation and per-subgroup evaluation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Perfect generalization:** a drop from 98% to 70% on unseen data is the opposite of good generalization.
- ✓ **B. Overfitting, worsened by under-represented groups (correct):** the large gap between training and new-data accuracy shows overfitting, and the group with few examples is where memorization hurts generalization the most.
- ✗ **C. Underfitting across all groups:** an underfit model scores poorly on the training data too, not 98%.
- ✗ **D. Too much training data:** more data usually reduces overfitting, and the scenario explicitly says the worst group had too few examples.

## Key idea
High training accuracy with low accuracy on new data means overfitting, and sparse subgroups are hit hardest.
Q000108:
## Two different quality checks in the ML lifecycle
- **Label quality analysis** looks at the training data itself. It checks whether human annotators agree with each other and with guidelines, for example by measuring inter-annotator agreement, reviewing disagreements and auditing a sample of labels. Services such as Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth use multiple workers per item and annotation consolidation to improve label accuracy.
- **Subgroup analysis** looks at the model's outputs. It compares metrics such as accuracy or false positive rate across demographic segments to detect unequal performance; SageMaker Clarify can compute these bias metrics and monitor them after deployment.
## Matching task to technique
Task (1) is about annotators and labels, which is a data-quality question. Task (2) is about model performance across segments in production, which is a subgroup comparison. The order in the answer must match that order.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Subgroup analysis, then hyperparameter tuning:** subgroup analysis does not check annotator labels, and hyperparameter tuning optimizes training settings rather than measuring performance across groups.
- ✓ **B. Label quality analysis, then subgroup analysis (correct):** annotator consistency is checked by analyzing label quality, and performance differences across demographic segments are checked by subgroup analysis.
- ✗ **C. Subgroup analysis, then label quality analysis:** both techniques are right but in reverse order; labels are task (1) and segment performance is task (2).
- ✗ **D. A/B testing, then label quality analysis:** A/B testing compares two variants with live traffic, not annotator consistency, and label analysis does not measure performance per demographic segment.

## Key idea
Check the labels with label quality analysis and check fairness of outcomes with subgroup analysis.
Q000109:
## How Bedrock Guardrails filter content
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluate prompts and model responses at inference time. Content filters cover categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence, misconduct and prompt attacks, each with a configurable strength (for example low, medium or high).
## The safety versus helpfulness tradeoff
- A **higher** filter strength blocks more borderline content, which lowers the risk of harmful output but also increases **false positives**: legitimate questions that happen to resemble a risky category get blocked.
- A **lower** strength lets more through, improving helpfulness but raising the risk of harmful replies.
Example: a pharmacy chatbot with maximum violence and misconduct filters might block "What is the lethal dose of acetaminophen?" even when asked for safety reasons.
Teams tune strengths per category, test with realistic prompts, and review blocked requests to find a balance that fits their use case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No effect on user experience:** the complaints in the scenario show the opposite; what gets blocked or redacted directly shapes what users can do.
- ✗ **B. Guardrails only affect training:** guardrails are applied at inference to prompts and responses; they are not a training-time setting, so they can and do cause the blocking users see.
- ✓ **C. Aggressive filtering reduces usability (correct):** very strict filters catch benign requests as well as harmful ones, so users lose helpful answers, which is the classic tradeoff between safety and helpfulness.
- ✗ **D. Guardrails auto-resolve the tradeoff:** guardrails do not pick a balance for you; you choose filter strengths and policies and must tune them for your use case.

## Key idea
Stronger safety filters mean more false positives, so tune guardrails to balance protection with usefulness.
Q000110:
## Guardrail policy types in Amazon Bedrock
- **Denied topics**: you describe a subject in natural language (a name, a definition and optional sample phrases), and the guardrail detects prompts or responses about that subject, even when phrased indirectly.
- **Content filters**: detect harmful categories such as hate, violence, sexual content, insults and misconduct, plus prompt attacks.
- **Word filters**: block exact words or phrases, including profanity or a custom list.
- **Sensitive information filters**: detect and block or mask PII.
- **Contextual grounding checks**: flag responses that are not supported by the provided source or not relevant to the query.
## Why a topic definition beats a word list
"Should I move my savings into index funds or bonds?" contains no forbidden keyword like "invest", but it is still a request for investment advice. A denied topic defined as "personalized recommendations about buying or selling financial products" catches it because it is evaluated on meaning.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Contextual grounding checks:** these check that a response is grounded in the supplied source and relevant to the query; they do not stop the assistant from discussing a forbidden subject.
- ✗ **B. Word filters for investment terms:** exact-match word lists miss indirect phrasing that avoids the listed terms, and they can over-block harmless uses of those words.
- ✓ **C. Denied topics with a definition and examples (correct):** a denied topic is matched on the meaning of the subject, so the assistant refuses investment advice even when users avoid obvious keywords.
- ✗ **D. Violence content filters:** the violence category targets violent content; investment advice is not violent, so this filter would not trigger.

## Key idea
Use denied topics to block a subject by meaning; word filters only match specific words.
Q000111:
## Right-sizing a model
Bigger foundation models are not automatically better for a given task. Larger models need more compute per request, which raises cost, latency and energy use.
## A responsible selection process
- Define the business requirement and an evaluation set first (for example, "classify support tickets into 12 categories with at least 90% accuracy").
- Evaluate several candidates, including smaller or task-specific models, using tools such as Amazon Bedrock model evaluation.
- Pick the smallest model that meets the requirement; consider prompt engineering or RAG before fine-tuning, and fine-tuning an existing model before training from scratch.
Example: a smaller model that reaches the accuracy target at a fraction of the per-token price is the better choice over a much larger model that is only slightly more accurate on this task.
Using fewer compute resources also reduces environmental impact, which AWS lists as a sustainability consideration.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Evaluate smaller or task-specific models that meet needs (correct):** choosing the smallest model that satisfies the requirements lowers cost and energy use while still delivering the business outcome.
- ✗ **B. Retrain an FM from scratch per use case:** pre-training a foundation model takes huge amounts of data, compute and energy, which contradicts both the budget and the environmental goal.
- ✗ **C. Always the highest parameter count:** the largest model maximizes cost and energy per request, and may bring no measurable benefit for the task.
- ✗ **D. Choose by brand recognition:** brand says nothing about fit, cost or efficiency for this use case; responsible selection is based on evaluation against requirements.

## Key idea
Choose the smallest model that meets the requirement; bigger or brand-new models add cost and energy without guaranteed benefit.
Q000112:
## Bias and variance as error types
- **High bias**: the model is too simple or has learned a skewed pattern, so its errors are **systematic**. It is wrong in the same direction again and again.
- **High variance**: the model is overly sensitive to its training data, so its predictions are **erratic**. Small differences in input can swing the output widely.
## Why both matter for responsible AI
- Model A consistently underpredicts approvals for one group regardless of qualifications. That systematic error means one group is predictably disadvantaged: a fairness harm that is directional.
- Model B gives wildly different results for similar applicants. That inconsistency undermines reliability and fair treatment for everyone, since two equally qualified people may get opposite outcomes.
Both are responsible AI concerns, but they show up differently and are fixed differently (for example richer features or rebalanced data for bias, regularization or more data for variance).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Not relevant to responsible AI:** both conditions directly affect whether people are treated fairly and reliably, so they are core responsible AI concerns, not purely academic statistics.
- ✗ **B. Identical fairness effects:** one produces a directional, systematic disadvantage for a group and the other produces random inconsistency; the effects differ.
- ✗ **C. Variance always discriminatory, bias never:** this reverses the scenario; the systematic disadvantage to a group comes from high bias, and high variance is not automatically discriminatory.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Bias disadvantages a group systematically; variance is erratic: high bias produces a consistent, predictable skew against one group, while high variance produces unreliable, inconsistent decisions for similar applicants.

## Key idea
High bias means systematic, predictable harm to a group; high variance means inconsistent, unreliable decisions.
Q000113:
## Transparency in responsible AI
Transparency means stakeholders can find out what a model is, how it was built and where it should not be trusted. Typical questions:
- What is the model meant to do, and what is it not meant to do?
- What data was it trained and evaluated on?
- How well does it perform, and what are its known limitations and risks?
## Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
SageMaker Model Cards are a structured document attached to a model that records intended uses, risk rating, training details, evaluation results and caveats. They can be exported (for example to PDF) and shared with auditors or regulators.
- Example: a card for a loan-risk model lists its training data period, the metrics per segment and "not validated for small-business loans" as a limitation.
AWS AI Service Cards serve a similar purpose for AWS's own AI services.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Latency; CloudWatch dashboards:** latency is a performance measure, and dashboards show operational metrics, not training data or limitations.
- ✗ **B. Scalability; Auto Scaling policies:** scaling policies describe how capacity grows with load, which tells a regulator nothing about how the model decides or what it was trained on.
- ✓ **C. Transparency; Model Cards (correct):** the regulator is asking how the model works, what trained it and its limits, which is transparency, and a model card is the artifact that records exactly that.
- ✗ **D. Cost; AWS Budgets:** Budgets tracks spend against thresholds; cost is not the concept being asked about and budgets contain no model documentation.

## Key idea
Questions about how a model works and its limits are transparency questions, answered with model documentation such as SageMaker Model Cards.
Q000114:
## Documenting a model versus monitoring or controlling it
Different AWS tools cover different parts of governing a model:
- **Amazon SageMaker Model Cards**: a single, versioned record of a model's intended uses, training data, evaluation metrics, risk rating and known limitations. Designed for review, approval and audit.
- **Amazon CloudWatch**: collects runtime metrics and logs, such as endpoint latency and error counts.
- **AWS CloudTrail**: records API calls made in the account, such as who created or deleted an endpoint.
- **Amazon Bedrock Guardrails**: enforces safety policies on prompts and responses of generative AI applications.
## Why documentation matters
Reviewers need to judge whether a model is appropriate for a use and what could go wrong. A model card gives them that context in one place, and SageMaker Model Dashboard can show model cards alongside monitoring status.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bedrock Guardrails:** guardrails filter and block content at inference time for generative AI apps; they do not document a model's data, metrics or intended uses.
- ✗ **B. AWS CloudTrail:** CloudTrail logs who called which API and when, which helps audit actions but does not describe the model itself.
- ✗ **C. Amazon CloudWatch:** CloudWatch tracks operational metrics and logs such as latency and errors, not the model's intended uses or training sources.
- ✓ **D. Amazon SageMaker Model Cards (correct):** they are built specifically to record intended use, training data sources, performance metrics and limitations so reviewers and auditors can evaluate a model.

## Key idea
To document what a model is for and its limits, use SageMaker Model Cards; logs and metrics describe activity, not the model.
Q000115:
## Transparency is valuable but not unlimited
Transparency helps regulators, customers and auditors trust an AI system. But some systems are **adversarial**: people actively try to defeat them.
## Why fraud detection is a special case
A fraud model works partly because fraudsters do not know exactly which signals it uses.
- If the company publishes that transactions under a certain amount from new devices are rarely flagged, fraudsters can shape their behavior to stay under that line.
- Publishing training data could also expose sensitive customer information.
## Balancing the two
Companies usually give regulators detailed information through controlled channels (confidential filings, audits, model documentation with restricted access) while sharing only high-level descriptions publicly. The goal is enough transparency for accountability without handing attackers a map for evasion.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disclosure has no security effect:** knowing how a detector works is exactly what helps attackers design inputs that avoid it, which is the reviewers' concern.
- ✗ **B. Regulators never require transparency:** the scenario itself starts with regulators wanting transparency, and regulated industries commonly require explanation and documentation of models.
- ✗ **C. Always perfectly aligned:** this scenario shows a direct conflict; more disclosure improves accountability but weakens the system's resistance to abuse.
- ✓ **D. Transparency can conflict with safety and security goals (correct):** full public disclosure of a fraud model's architecture and data could help bad actors evade it, so openness has to be balanced against security.

## Key idea
More transparency is not always safer; in adversarial systems it must be balanced with security.
Q000116:
## "Open" does not mean "no conditions"
Open-source and open-weight foundation models are released under licenses, and those licenses differ a lot.
- Some permissive licenses (for example Apache 2.0) allow commercial use with attribution and notice requirements.
- Some model-specific licenses add acceptable-use policies, restrict certain uses, or set conditions for very large deployments.
## What the model card adds
A model card (or model documentation) describes intended uses, training data, evaluation results, known limitations, and risks such as bias or unsafe outputs. Reading it tells you whether the model is suitable for your use case and what testing you still need.
## A responsible adoption checklist
- Read the license and confirm your use is allowed and what attribution is required.
- Read the model card for intended use and limitations.
- Evaluate the model on your own data and risk cases before launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove attribution:** many licenses require attribution and notices, so removing them can breach the license terms.
- ✗ **B. Skip evaluation because it is popular:** popularity does not show the model performs well or safely on your specific data and use case.
- ✗ **C. Assume open source means no restrictions:** open models carry licenses with conditions such as attribution or acceptable-use limits that still apply.
- ✓ **D. Review the license and model card (correct):** the license defines what you are legally allowed to do, and the model card tells you what the model is suited for and where it is weak.

## Key idea
Before building on an open model, read its license and model card and evaluate it yourself.
Q000117:
## Human-centered design for AI systems
Human-centered design puts the people using a system at the center: they should understand what the AI is doing, be able to question it, and have their experience feed back into improvements.
## Feedback as part of explainability
- A thumbs up or down, a rating, or a "report this answer" button gives users a voice when a response is confusing or wrong.
- Flagged responses can be reviewed by humans, used to find where explanations or answers fall short, and added to evaluation or tuning data.
- It also signals to users that responses are AI-generated and open to correction, which builds appropriate trust.
Example: a support bot shows "Was this answer helpful?" under each reply and links flagged conversations to a review queue.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. A way for users to flag or rate responses (correct):** it keeps a human in the loop, lets users signal when output is unclear or wrong, and gives the team data to improve the chatbot's answers and explanations.
- ✗ **B. Remove user-facing explanations:** this reduces users' understanding of the AI's output, which works against explainability.
- ✗ **C. Disable logging of interactions:** without logs there is no record to review or learn from, so problems users hit cannot be investigated or fixed.
- ✗ **D. Restrict access to employees:** limiting who can use the chatbot avoids customers rather than designing the experience around them.

## Key idea
Human-centered design means giving users a way to respond to AI output, such as flagging or rating it.
Q000118:
## Two levels of transparency
- **Model-level (global)**: what the model is for, what data trained it, how it performs overall, and its known limitations. A SageMaker Model Card documents this.
- **Prediction-level (local)**: why the model produced a particular output for a particular input. This needs a per-prediction explanation method.
## Per-prediction explanations
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) assigns each input feature a contribution score for one prediction. Amazon SageMaker Clarify can compute these feature attributions.
- Example: for one denied loan application, SHAP might show `debt_to_income` pushed the score down strongly while `years_employed` pushed it up slightly.
A model card cannot contain this, because it is written once for the model, not generated for each customer. Regulated decisions often need both levels.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cards track billing and cost:** model cards document intended use, training, evaluation and risk; they are not a cost-tracking tool.
- ✓ **B. Model cards describe the model, not individual predictions (correct):** the card documents overall purpose, data and limits, while explaining one customer's denial requires a prediction-level method such as Clarify feature attribution.
- ✗ **C. Cards auto-generate per-prediction explanations:** a model card is a static document for the whole model and does not produce an explanation for each inference.
- ✗ **D. Functionally identical, no gap:** model-level documentation and per-prediction explanations answer different questions, which is exactly the gap the data scientist raised.

## Key idea
A model card explains the model as a whole; explaining one specific decision needs prediction-level feature attribution.
Q000119:
## Feature attribution
Feature attribution explains a model's output by showing how much each input feature contributed to it.
- **Global** attribution ranks which features matter most across the whole dataset.
- **Local** attribution explains one individual prediction.
## SageMaker Clarify and SHAP
Amazon SageMaker Clarify computes feature attributions using a SHAP-based method (Kernel SHAP). SHAP values show, for a given record, how each feature pushed the prediction up or down from a baseline.
- Example: for a customer flagged as likely to churn, Clarify might show `support_tickets_last_30_days` contributed most, followed by `contract_months_remaining`.
Clarify can run these explanations in processing jobs, provide online explainability for endpoints, and monitor attribution drift over time with SageMaker Model Monitor.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. SageMaker Clarify feature attribution (correct):** it computes SHAP-based per-record attributions that show which features most influenced that customer's prediction, which is what is needed to explain the decision.
- ✗ **B. AWS Cost Explorer:** Cost Explorer analyzes AWS spending and usage trends; it has no view into how a model weighed input features.
- ✗ **C. AWS Trusted Advisor:** Trusted Advisor checks an account against best practices in areas such as cost optimization, security, performance and service quotas; it does not explain model predictions.
- ✗ **D. CloudWatch Logs Insights:** Logs Insights queries log data you already wrote; it cannot compute feature contributions for a model's prediction.

## Key idea
To explain why a model made a specific prediction, use SageMaker Clarify feature attribution (SHAP).
Q000120:
## Transparency toward end users
Transparency is not only for regulators. People using an AI system should know when they are interacting with AI and where its information comes from.
## Common disclosure practices
- Labeling replies as AI-generated, for example "Generated by AI".
- Citing or naming the data sources used; RAG applications such as those built on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can return source citations with an answer.
- Stating known limitations, such as "may be inaccurate; verify important details".
## Why it matters
Users who know an answer is AI-generated and see its sources can calibrate their trust, double-check critical information, and choose to contact a human. Hiding AI involvement can mislead users and damage trust when errors surface.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reduced inference cost:** adding a label or a source list does not change how much the model costs to run; if anything it adds a little text.
- ✗ **B. Faster response time:** disclosure text does not make generation faster; latency depends on the model, prompt size and output length.
- ✓ **C. Transparency to users about AI content (correct):** telling users that replies are AI-generated and which sources they draw on is a direct application of transparency.
- ✗ **D. Robustness to noisy inputs:** robustness is about stable behavior under typos or rephrasing; labeling output has no effect on how the model handles messy input.

## Key idea
Disclosing AI involvement and sources to users is transparency, not a performance or robustness measure.
Q000121:
## The interpretability versus accuracy tradeoff
- **Interpretable models** such as rules-based scorecards, linear or logistic regression and small decision trees are easy to explain: each input's effect on the result is visible.
- **Complex models** such as deep neural networks can capture more subtle patterns and are often more accurate, but their internal reasoning is hard to inspect.
## Options in a regulated industry
Credit decisions often require that applicants be told the main reasons for a denial. A company can:
- Choose the interpretable model and accept slightly lower accuracy, or
- Keep the deep learning model and add post-hoc explainability tooling, such as SHAP feature attributions from Amazon SageMaker Clarify, then validate that the explanations meet regulatory needs.
Either way, the decision is a deliberate tradeoff that depends on the regulation, the accuracy gap and the risk of each approach.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Deep learning always more accurate and more interpretable:** deep models are generally less interpretable, which is precisely why a tradeoff exists.
- ✗ **B. Rules apply only to rules-based models:** explainability obligations apply to the decision, regardless of which model technique produced it.
- ✗ **C. Interpretability and accuracy unrelated to model choice:** model choice largely determines how interpretable the system is and how accurate it can be.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Accept slightly lower accuracy or add explainability tooling for the DNN: this names the real tradeoff and the two practical ways to meet strict explainability rules.

## Key idea
Regulated decisions force a choice between simpler, explainable models and more accurate opaque models backed by explainability tools.
Q000122:
## Intended use and out-of-scope use
A key purpose of a model card is to tell others what the model is and is not for.
- **Intended uses**: the tasks, populations and conditions the model was built and validated for.
- **Out-of-scope uses**: uses the owners explicitly advise against because the model was not tested for them or could cause harm.
## What goes wrong without it
Example: a resume-screening model validated for entry-level engineering roles is reused by another team to rank candidates for executive positions. The data, features and evaluation never covered that case, so results are poor and possibly unfair.
SageMaker Model Cards include an intended-uses section with fields for the purpose, intended uses, factors affecting performance and risk rating. Filling it in, and saying clearly what the model must not be used for, gives other teams the information to avoid misuse.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More decimal places on accuracy:** extra precision on one metric does not tell anyone which tasks the model is suited for.
- ✗ **B. Larger font size:** formatting changes readability, not content; the missing information about intended use would still be missing.
- ✗ **C. Translate into more languages:** translating an incomplete card spreads the same gap to more readers without adding the missing guidance.
- ✓ **D. Document intended and out-of-scope uses (correct):** stating what the model was validated for and what it should not be used for would have warned the other team that its purpose was out of scope.

## Key idea
Model cards prevent misuse by stating both intended and out-of-scope uses.
Q000123:
## What Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provide
Guardrails is a set of configurable safeguards applied to the prompts and responses of generative AI applications. One guardrail can combine several policies:
- **Denied topics**: refuse subjects such as investment advice, defined in natural language.
- **Content filters**: detect and block harmful categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence and misconduct, plus prompt attacks.
- **Sensitive information filters**: detect PII types or custom regex patterns (for example an account number format) and either block them or mask them in the output.
- **Contextual grounding checks**: score whether a response is grounded in the supplied source and relevant to the query, and block ungrounded ones.
- **Word filters**, and automated reasoning checks for some use cases.
Guardrails can be attached to model invocations, agents and knowledge bases, or called separately with the `ApplyGuardrail` API.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CloudWatch dashboards:** dashboards visualize metrics about the application after the fact; they cannot refuse topics, block hate speech or mask data in a response.
- ✗ **B. Bedrock fine-tuning:** fine-tuning shifts a model's style or knowledge but does not provide enforceable, configurable rules for blocking topics or masking account numbers.
- ✓ **C. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (correct):** denied topics, content filters, sensitive information masking and contextual grounding checks cover all four requirements in one place.
- ✗ **D. Bedrock Agents action groups:** action groups let an agent call APIs or Lambda functions to complete tasks; they are for taking actions, not enforcing content policies.

## Key idea
Policy controls on generative AI input and output, such as topics, harmful content, PII masking and grounding, belong in Bedrock Guardrails.
Q000124:
## Shared responsibility for managed ML
The AWS shared responsibility model splits security duties:
- **AWS: security OF the cloud**: physical data centers, hardware, the global network, and the virtualization layer (hypervisor). For a managed service such as Amazon SageMaker AI, AWS also operates the underlying service infrastructure.
- **Customer: security IN the cloud**: who can access what, how data is protected, and how services are configured.
## Customer tasks for a custom model on SageMaker AI
- Grant least-privilege access with IAM roles and policies for users, notebooks and training jobs.
- Encrypt training data and model artifacts (for example S3 with AWS KMS keys) and enable encryption for training volumes and traffic where needed.
- Configure networking such as running jobs in a VPC, and classify and govern the data used.
Example: an S3 bucket of training data left public is a customer failure, not an AWS one.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Patching the hypervisor:** the virtualization layer is AWS infrastructure that customers never access, so AWS patches it.
- ✗ **B. Maintaining global network hardware:** AWS owns and maintains the physical network across its Regions and edge locations.
- ✓ **C. IAM permissions and data encryption (correct):** controlling access to the model and data and choosing how data is encrypted are customer responsibilities under shared responsibility.
- ✗ **D. Physical security of data centers:** AWS controls data center access, guards and facilities; customers have no physical access.

## Key idea
AWS secures the infrastructure; the customer secures access, data and configuration of what they build on it.
Q000125:
## Amazon Macie in brief
Amazon Macie is a data security service that uses machine learning and pattern matching to **discover sensitive data in Amazon S3**.
- **Managed data identifiers** detect common sensitive types such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, names and addresses.
- **Custom data identifiers** let you add your own regex patterns, such as internal customer IDs.
- **Sensitive data discovery jobs** scan chosen buckets and produce findings that show which objects contain which types of sensitive data; Macie also evaluates bucket security posture (for example public access).
## Why this matters before fine-tuning
Data used to fine-tune a model can influence its outputs, so PII left in the training set could end up exposed in generated text. Scanning transcripts with Macie first lets the team redact, mask or remove those records before training.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Amazon Macie (correct):** it is purpose-built to scan S3 objects and flag sensitive data like credit card and Social Security numbers, which is exactly the pre-training check required.
- ✗ **B. AWS Config:** Config records and evaluates resource configurations, such as whether a bucket has encryption enabled; it does not read file contents to find PII.
- ✗ **C. AWS Trusted Advisor:** Trusted Advisor gives account-level best-practice checks for areas such as cost, security and service quotas; it does not inspect data inside objects.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector scans workloads and code (EC2 instances, container images, Lambda functions and connected code repositories) for software vulnerabilities and exposure; it does not search S3 data for sensitive content.

## Key idea
To find PII inside S3 data before training, use Amazon Macie; Config, Inspector and Trusted Advisor check configurations or vulnerabilities, not data contents.
Q000126:
## How a VPC normally reaches AWS APIs
Amazon Bedrock is called through regional HTTPS endpoints such as `bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`. By default those names resolve to public IP addresses, so an instance in a private subnet needs an internet gateway or a NAT gateway to reach them.
## Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink)
An interface VPC endpoint places elastic network interfaces with private IPs from your own subnets into the VPC. With private DNS enabled, the normal Bedrock hostname resolves to those private IPs, so the SDK code does not change.
- Traffic goes from the app to the endpoint's private IP and then over the AWS network to Bedrock, never across the public internet.
- Bedrock offers endpoint services such as `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime` for inference and `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock` for control-plane calls.
- You can attach an endpoint policy and security groups to limit who uses the endpoint and which actions are allowed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. PrivateLink interface endpoint for Bedrock (correct):** it gives the VPC a private path to the Bedrock APIs, so subnets need no internet gateway or NAT route and the isolation requirement is met.
- ✗ **B. Internet gateway with security groups:** security groups only filter which ports and destinations are allowed; the allowed traffic still goes out through the internet gateway to the public Bedrock endpoint.
- ✗ **C. CloudFront in front of Bedrock:** CloudFront is a content delivery network for serving content to clients at the edge. It does not give a VPC a private route to an AWS API, and requests would still go over public networking.
- ✗ **D. NAT gateway:** a NAT gateway lets private-subnet instances start outbound connections, but it forwards them through an internet gateway to the public endpoint, which is the path the company wants to avoid.

## Key idea
Private access from a VPC to an AWS API means an interface (PrivateLink) endpoint; NAT and internet gateways both lead to the public internet path.
Q000127:
## Why RAG needs data lineage
In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app, source documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings and stored in a vector index. When an answer is questioned in a compliance review, you need to know which document, and which version of it, produced the chunk the model used.
## Catalogs and metadata
A data catalog stores metadata about datasets: where they live, their schema, owners, versions and custom properties.
- The AWS Glue Data Catalog holds table and dataset definitions, including their Amazon S3 locations and schemas, and crawlers can keep them up to date as data changes.
- You can add custom properties such as source system, document version and ingestion date to catalog entries, and record the same identifiers as metadata on each chunk in the vector store.
- Example: a chunk tagged `doc=policy-17, version=4` can be matched to the catalog entry that describes the source dataset and its S3 location used for the embedding run.
For end-to-end lineage graphs, AWS also offers lineage features in Amazon SageMaker Catalog (Amazon DataZone), which build on catalog metadata; among the listed options, only the Glue Data Catalog addresses cataloging at all.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CloudWatch Logs Insights:** it queries log events such as application or invocation logs. It can show that a request happened, but it does not keep a catalog of source datasets and their versions.
- ✗ **B. Bedrock Guardrails:** guardrails filter prompts and responses for harmful content, denied topics or sensitive information. They do not record where training or retrieval data came from.
- ✓ **C. Glue Data Catalog with metadata tracking (correct):** it is the AWS service built to catalog datasets and their metadata, so recording source and version details there gives reviewers a record of which sources fed each embedding build.
- ✗ **D. AWS KMS:** KMS creates and controls encryption keys that protect data. It says nothing about which documents or versions a dataset contains.

## Key idea
Tracing outputs back to source data is a metadata and cataloging problem (Glue Data Catalog), not logging, content filtering or encryption.
Q000128:
## Agents act with an IAM role
An Amazon Bedrock agent calls tools through action groups, often AWS Lambda functions that in turn call internal APIs. Every call runs with the permissions of an IAM role, so the role, not the prompt, decides what the agent can actually do.
## Least privilege
Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources a job needs.
- For an order-status lookup, allow only read actions such as a `GetOrderStatus` API on the order resources.
- Leave out write actions like `CancelOrder` or `UpdateOrder`, so even a manipulated or confused agent cannot perform them.
- Prompt instructions are not a security boundary: prompt injection or model mistakes can make an agent try actions it was told to avoid.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Full access plus prompt instructions:** prompts can be bypassed by prompt injection or ignored by the model, and the full permissions would then let the agent change or cancel orders.
- ✗ **B. Shared IAM user credentials:** long-term keys shared across agents are hard to rotate, cannot be scoped per agent and make it impossible to tell which agent made a call. Agents should use their own roles with temporary credentials.
- ✓ **C. Least privilege, read-only actions (correct):** if the role can only read order status, modification or cancellation is impossible regardless of what the model generates.
- ✗ **D. AdministratorAccess:** this grants every action on every resource in the account, the opposite of the requirement, and turns any agent mistake into a possible account-wide incident.

## Key idea
Control what an agent can do with narrowly scoped IAM permissions, never with prompt instructions or broad access.
Q000129:
## Who did what, and when
Every change to an Amazon Bedrock guardrail is an API call, such as `UpdateGuardrail` or `CreateGuardrailVersion`. AWS CloudTrail records these management events with:
- the identity that made the call (IAM user, role session or federated user),
- the time, source IP address and user agent,
- the request parameters and the response.
## Where to look
CloudTrail event history shows the last 90 days of management events in a Region at no extra cost. For longer retention or analysis, a trail delivers the events to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs, and CloudTrail Lake can store and query them with SQL.
Example: filtering event history for event name `UpdateGuardrail` shows which role changed the content filter strength and at what time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CloudWatch Metrics:** metrics are numeric time series such as invocation counts or latency. They carry no information about which user made a configuration change.
- ✗ **B. Trusted Advisor:** it checks accounts against best practices for cost, security, resilience and limits. It does not keep an audit trail of individual API calls.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets. It does not track changes to Bedrock resources.
- ✓ **D. AWS CloudTrail (correct):** it records API activity with the caller identity and timestamp, which is exactly the evidence needed to find who weakened the guardrail and when.

## Key idea
Investigating who changed a resource starts with CloudTrail's API activity record; metrics, best-practice checks and data discovery do not identify callers.
Q000130:
## AWS's compliance evidence
Under the shared responsibility model, AWS is audited by third parties for the security of the cloud. The results are reports such as SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3, ISO 27001 certificates and PCI DSS attestations.
## AWS Artifact
AWS Artifact is a self-service portal in the AWS console for these documents.
- **Artifact Reports**: download AWS's audit reports and certifications on demand, often under a confidentiality agreement you accept in the console.
- **Artifact Agreements**: review and accept agreements such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA) for HIPAA.
Example: a customer's security questionnaire asks for proof of AWS's controls, so the company downloads the SOC 2 report from Artifact and shares it according to its terms.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Artifact (correct):** it is the official source for AWS's own compliance reports and certifications, including ISO 27001 and SOC 2.
- ✗ **B. AWS Config:** Config records and evaluates the configuration of your own resources. It says nothing about AWS's audited controls.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector scans your EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities; it does not provide audit reports.
- ✗ **D. Trusted Advisor:** it gives best-practice recommendations about your account, not third-party audit reports about AWS.

## Key idea
AWS's own audit reports come from AWS Artifact; Config, Inspector and Trusted Advisor assess your resources, not AWS's.
Q000131:
## Configuration compliance
AWS Config records the configuration of supported resources, such as S3 buckets, and keeps a history of changes. **Config rules** evaluate each resource against a desired setting and mark it `COMPLIANT` or `NON_COMPLIANT`.
## Managed rules for S3
AWS provides ready-made managed rules, for example:
- `s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled` checks that default encryption is set.
- `s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited` and `s3-bucket-public-write-prohibited` check that buckets do not allow public access.
Rules run when a resource changes or on a schedule, so a bucket that drifts is flagged soon after the change. You can add automatic remediation with Systems Manager Automation documents, and conformance packs group rules for many accounts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon GuardDuty:** GuardDuty detects threats from activity, such as unusual API calls or data access patterns. It is not a tool for checking that bucket settings match a required baseline.
- ✓ **B. AWS Config with managed rules (correct):** it continuously evaluates bucket settings against the encryption and public access requirements and flags any bucket that falls out of compliance.
- ✗ **C. AWS CloudTrail:** CloudTrail records who called which API. It shows that a bucket policy changed, but it does not evaluate whether the result is compliant.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector scans compute workloads for software vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not check S3 bucket encryption or public access settings.

## Key idea
Is this resource configured the way it should be, continuously? That is AWS Config rules, not threat detection or API logging.
Q000132:
## Two different security questions
- **Is the software on my instances vulnerable?** Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2 instances (and container images and Lambda functions) for known CVEs in installed packages. For EC2 it also reports network reachability findings, such as ports open to the internet.
- **Has my configuration changed from what we approved?** AWS Config records resource configurations, including security groups, and evaluates them with rules. A rule such as `restricted-ssh` or a custom rule can flag a security group that allows traffic outside the baseline.
## Example
Inspector reports that an inference instance runs an OpenSSL version with a known CVE. Separately, someone opens port 8080 to `0.0.0.0/0` on the endpoint's security group; Config records the change and marks the group non-compliant.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Trusted Advisor for both:** Trusted Advisor runs a fixed set of account-level best-practice checks. It does not scan instance software for CVEs or evaluate each change against your own approved baseline.
- ✓ **B. Inspector for vulnerabilities; Config for drift (correct):** each service matches its need exactly, Inspector finds CVEs and unintended exposure, and Config tracks security group changes against rules.
- ✗ **C. Config for vulnerabilities, Inspector for drift:** this swaps the roles. Config does not inspect installed packages for CVEs, and Inspector does not track configuration history or baselines.
- ✗ **D. Macie and Artifact:** Macie finds sensitive data in S3, and Artifact provides AWS compliance reports. Neither scans instances or detects security group drift.

## Key idea
Inspector answers "is it vulnerable?"; Config answers "is it still configured the way we approved?".
Q000133:
## AWS Trusted Advisor
Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS account and gives recommendations based on AWS best practices. Its checks are grouped into categories:
- **Cost optimization**: idle load balancers, underused EC2 instances, unassociated Elastic IPs.
- **Security**: S3 buckets with open access, security groups with unrestricted ports, MFA on the root user.
- **Fault tolerance**: EBS snapshots, single-AZ deployments.
- **Performance** and **service limits (quotas)**: resources approaching quota limits.
- **Operational excellence**.
All customers get the core security checks and the service quota checks; the full set of checks requires a higher-tier support plan, such as Business or Enterprise support.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Macie findings:** Macie reports sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets. It does not look at costs, resilience or quotas.
- ✓ **B. AWS Trusted Advisor (correct):** it gives ongoing best-practice recommendations across exactly the categories listed, cost, security, fault tolerance and service limits.
- ✗ **C. AWS Artifact:** Artifact is where you download AWS's compliance reports and accept agreements; it does not analyze your account.
- ✗ **D. AWS Audit Manager:** Audit Manager collects evidence and maps it to compliance frameworks for audits. It does not recommend cost savings or warn about service limits.

## Key idea
